extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of media studies and journalism; instructors analyzing news ideology and content
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and analytic criteria for identifying ideological influence in news coverage (propaganda filters, hegemony, routines, framing, and editorial normalization). Intended to guide content analysis and critical reading of news texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Herman & Chomsky: Ownership/Size/Profit Orientation (Filter 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The size, concentrated ownership, owner wealth, and profit orientation of the dominant mass media firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large, concentrated, profit-oriented ownership constrains what is newsworthy and makes alternative media difficult to sustain; examine ownership structures and profit incentives when assessing bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising as Primary Income Source (Filter 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising as the primary income source of the mass media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because advertisers are a major revenue source, content and formats that please advertisers or avoid offending them will be favored; evaluate story selection and framing for advertiser-friendly tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on Government, Business, and Approved 'Experts' (Filter 3 / Source Influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reliance of the media on information provided by government, business, and 'experts' funded and approved by these primary sources and agents of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for heavy use of official sources, PR materials, and industry-funded experts; note how government information staffs and corporate PR budgets subsidize reporting. Watch for routine dependence on such sources and for mechanisms (e.g., providing authoritative news, access, logistics) that make those voices dominant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flak as a Discipline Mechanism (Filter 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Flak' as negative responses to the media (complaints, threats, petitions, letters, articles) used to discipline the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify organized campaigns, think-tank or foundation-funded monitoring, and aggressive complaint strategies that push media toward certain lines. Note especially resource-backed flak originating from the political Right as described (e.g., Accuracy in Media).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticommunism as Ideological Control (Filter 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Anticommunism' as a national religion and control mechanism used instrumentally by elites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect ideological tropes that mark certain actors as deviant/enemy and justify double standards (e.g., supporting allies while attacking enemies); assess whether anticommunist (or analogous) frameworks are used to legitimize policy or marginalize opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda-model observable indicators: dichotomization and serviceability to power
rubrics_metrics.description: A propaganda approach suggests systematic and highly political dichotomization in news coverage based on service-ability to important domestic power interests; observable in choices of story and in the volume and quality of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure whether coverage privileges certain actors/issues (volume, prominence, tone, depth) while marginalizing others; compare quality and quantity of coverage for 'friends' vs 'enemies' of powerful interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covert/Planted Content and 'White Propaganda' Tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Government or other actors covertly plant favorable coverage (e.g., prepared op-eds, use of 'cut-outs', clandestine trips coordinated with reporters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of planted op-eds, commissioned pieces bearing third-party signatures, coordinated visits/briefings, or other 'cut-out' intermediaries that hide source involvement (e.g., State Department memo examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hegemony: production of commonsensical ideology and marginalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Media institutions serve a hegemonic function by continually producing a cohesive ideology — a set of commonsensical values and norms — that reproduces and legitimates the social structure while marginalizing voices outside elite circles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how frames, narratives, and repeated metaphors naturalize particular values; assess which meanings are presented as 'common sense' and which perspectives are delegitimized or excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routines aligning with hegemonic requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: News routines develop to meet hegemonic requirements, not just organizational needs; routines (e.g., source selection, framing) serve ideological ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how everyday news practices (beats, source reliance, deadlines, 'official' sourcing) systematically favor elite perspectives. Consider the sphere (consensus, legitimate controversy, deviance) in which routines operate and how routines differ by sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: News-paradigm emphasis on objectivity/accuracy/balance/fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: The journalistic paradigm privileges objectivity (or proximate standards: accuracy, balance, fairness) and discourages strongly held values as occupationally useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how claims of 'objectivity' are enacted (e.g., by privileging prominent sources) and whether those practices function to maintain elite-defined boundaries rather than produce independent critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: False balance: using 'balance' to create a centrist middle ground
rubrics_metrics.description: The routine of 'balancing' sources can be applied as a formula to create a presumed middle ground, even when the sides are unequal (e.g., making a much larger antiwar crowd appear equal to a small pro-war group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare raw footage/data to final stories for selective editing, choice of soundbites, juxtaposition, and numerical misrepresentation. Identify when balance is formal rather than proportional or substantive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing by symbolic linking (e.g., 'support the troops', patriotism)
rubrics_metrics.description: News often links policy-supporting positions to positive symbols (the troops, patriotism, families) and distances or stigmatizes critics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for narrative and visual strategies that associate one side with communal values and human-interest figures to confer legitimacy; note which voices are given sympathetic, personalized treatment (e.g., named family members) versus which are abstracted or caricatured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local news and emotional/community appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Local television amplifies cultural and economic imperatives of audience appeal, often using emotional stories and community symbols to reproduce supportive attitudes toward policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess use of local frames, symbolic rituals, and emotionally resonant storytelling that foster community solidarity and support for official policy (e.g., presenting rallies as 'images of Americana').

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial gatekeeping and normalization of paradigm limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors internalize the journalistic paradigm and enforce limits (e.g., demanding inclusion of mainstream authorities, forbidding 'shrilly' or polemical tones); paradigm violations are 'repaired' or normalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine editorial interventions (requests to add conservative spokespeople, humorous framing of radical ideas) and the conditions under which editors accept or suppress dissenting frames. Note that factual correctness may protect a reporter even while ideological challenges are constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial newsworthiness criteria: significance, controversy, color, surprise; non-polemical tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are tolerated when they meet commercial journalistic standards for relevance and readability (significance, controversy, color, surprise) and adhere to a calm, matter-of-fact, non-polemical tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a story's acceptability within mainstream outlets, assess whether it displays these attributes and whether contentious perspectives are incorporated via mainstream authorities to confer respectability.
